summary: Under Cyrus, Daniel — honored above all the king's friends — dismantles two gods in one day. Bel, the idol that 'eats' twelve measures of flour, forty sheep, and six vessels of wine daily, is exposed when Daniel strews ashes on the temple floor: by morning, footprints of 'men, women, and children' lead to the priests' secret door. The great dragon, worshipped as living, bursts asunder from cakes of boiled pitch, fat, and hair. For this, Babylon forces the king to throw Daniel to seven lions — where an angel carries the prophet Habakkuk from Judea, dinner in hand. On the seventh day the king finds Daniel alive and confesses: 'Great art thou, O Lord God of Daniel, and there is none other beside thee.'
whyItMatters: This is the Bible's sharpest piece of idol-smashing satire — an argument carried by evidence rather than thunder. Its method (test the claim, follow the footprints) and its goal (a pagan king's confession) make it a compact apologetic: what you worship must be alive, or it is only 'clay within, and brass without.'

context.author: Unknown; Greek addition to Daniel, in circulation by the 2nd-1st century BC
context.date: Set in the reign of Cyrus of Persia (6th century BC); composed in the Greek period
context.setting: Babylon — the temple of Bel, the dragon's pit, the lions' den

outline.heading: The question put to Daniel

keyVerses.text: Because I may not worship idols made with hands, but the living God, who hath created the heaven and the earth, and hath sovereignty over all flesh.
keyVerses.why: Daniel's whole theology in one sentence — the line that divides every god in the chapter from the God who saves.

keyVerses.text: Then Daniel smiled, and said, O king, be not deceived: for this is but clay within, and brass without, and did never eat or drink any thing.
keyVerses.why: The smile is the argument — satire as theology. The test of a god: does it eat, or is it eaten?

keyVerses.text: And the king said, I see the footsteps of men, women, and children. And then the king was angry.
keyVerses.why: The forensic moment — the idol's divinity disproved by its own maintenance staff's footprints.

keyVerses.text: Then cried the king with a loud voice, saying, Great art thou, O Lord God of Daniel, and there is none other beside thee.
keyVerses.why: The chapter's goal reached: the confession Daniel's smile was aimed at all along.

questions.question: Why does this book exist separately when Daniel 14 tells the same story?
questions.answer: The Greek tradition transmitted the Daniel additions in two arrangements — attached to Daniel (where Bel and the Dragon is chapter 14) and as independent books. This arrangement keeps the Septuagint's separate books: Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Letter of Jeremiah each stand alone. Same tale, two shelves.

questions.question: Why does the story open with Cyrus instead of Darius?
questions.answer: The Septuagint's version opens with Astyages; the version behind this text begins with Cyrus receiving the kingdom. The two Greek forms of the additions differ in such details — a sign of popular tales circulating in more than one telling, not competing histories. Daniel 6's den is Darius's; this one is Cyrus's.

questions.question: Is the humor irreverent?
questions.answer: The story laughs at idols, never at God — the same line Elijah walks on Carmel when he suggests Baal is asleep or traveling. Daniel 'smiles' and 'laughs' (1:7, 1:19), the dragon bursts from indigestion, and the king ends by praising Daniel's God. Biblical satire has a long tradition; this is its purest specimen.

questions.question: What is the argument against Bel, exactly?
questions.answer: An argument from consumption: the priests claim Bel eats the offerings; Daniel claims the food is eaten by people. The sealed room and the ashes turn theology into forensics — and the footprints decide. The deeper point: a god that requires feeding is a dependent, not a deity. Only the God who 'hath created the heaven and the earth' gives rather than takes.

questions.question: Why is Habakkuk the delivery man?
questions.answer: The tale borrows a famous prophet for a famous miracle: carried by the hair from Judea to Babylon 'in the force of his spirit,' dinner in hand (1:35-36). Daniel's response — 'Thou hast remembered me, O God' — makes the point: God feeds his servants through surprising couriers. Rubens painted the scene; it remains one of Scripture's strangest and most beloved images.

glossary.def: 'Lord' — the Babylonian god Marduk, whose daily 'meals' the temple priesthood consumed.
The Persian king who conquered Babylon (539 BC); Daniel's patron here.
The prophet, airlifted from Judea with bread and pottage.
Tar, boiled with fat and hair into the lumps that burst the dragon.
